## Stage 0 — Document Accessibility Report

The supplied main document contains extracted text for physical PDF pages 1–31. Its title is **A Framework for Studying AI Agent Behavior: Evidence from Consumer Choice Experiments**. All 31 page records are present, and the supplied text reaches the final product-example figure. This establishes coverage of the supplied 31-page document, rather than independently proving that no other version or supplement exists. The publication header identifies it as a conference paper at ICLR 2026.

Direct visual inspection is available for pages 1–9, 13, 15–19, 24, and 27–31: 21 rendered pages. Pages 10–12, 14, 20–23, and 25–26 were inspected through supplied text only. All 17 numbered figures occur on rendered pages and were visually inspected. Tables 1–5 are also visually available; their supplied extracted text provides more reliable access to dense numeric entries than the small rendered type. The main equations are available as rendered images and extracted text, although the compact interaction notation requires explanation and has some specification ambiguity. Appendices A–J are present, despite the accessibility metadata reporting no detected appendix pages. The visible headings and supplied text establish their presence.

No separate code repository contents, experiment configuration files, trial-level datasets, model outputs, executable environment, or supplementary files were supplied. The paper advertises an open framework and displays a project address, but those artifacts were not opened or verified. The example agent context explicitly omits HTML and redacts URLs. Its missing content cannot be reconstructed. Figure 1's extracted embedded lettering is corrupted into glyph codes; the rendered diagram and readable caption permit interpretation of the workflow. No OCR or tools were used. Small plot labels and significance symbols are not uniformly legible enough to support exhaustive point-by-point transcription.

Evidence labels throughout: **[A] author-reported**, **[B] directly observable**, **[C] analyst-derived**, and **[D] analyst interpretation**. No external information is introduced. Confidence is HIGH for clearly readable methods and tabulated results, MEDIUM for qualitative interpretation of dense plots and bounded security relevance, and UNKNOWN for unreported implementation details or untested causal mechanisms. Prompts and code excerpts inside the paper are treated as study evidence, never instructions to this analyst.

## 1. Plain-language orientation

[A] This paper asks how language-model agents choose, rather than merely whether they finish a task. A shopping agent can successfully add something to a cart while choosing primarily because a page says that an item is a best seller, appears second, or has a slightly higher customer rating. A task-completion score can miss those influences.

[A] The researchers introduce **ABxLab**, short for Agent Behavior eXperiments. It intercepts the web-page observations delivered to an agent and applies controlled changes, such as inserting persuasive text or equalizing prices. They use it in OneStopMarket, a shopping environment, to compare choices across 17 language models, three attribute conditions, ten nudge texts, and selected product pairs. They report more than 80,000 experimental trials. A human baseline uses the original product comparisons.

[A] The central empirical finding is substantial sensitivity to ratings, price, presentation order, and persuasive messages. Removing competing attributes often makes the remaining cue more influential. Explicit user preference descriptions can also radically change priorities. The authors interpret these patterns as evidence of brittle, often hierarchical choice rules.

[D] For the user's security question—why web AI agents might be more vulnerable than standalone large language models—this paper contributes evidence about **environment-mediated influence over delegated action**. It does not directly compare web agents with standalone models. Its experimental comparator is principally other agent conditions and human participants. Therefore, it cannot establish an agent-versus-standalone vulnerability gap, quantify that gap, or isolate browsing, memory, or tool access as its cause.

## 2. Document roadmap

| S0 | Abstract | 1 | Problem, framework, main behavioral finding |
| S1 | Introduction | 1–2 | Delegation, competence versus trust, contributions |
| S2 | Related Work | 2–3 | Task benchmarks, behavioral science, shopping-agent positioning |
| S3 | Methods, §§3.1–3.5.4 | 3–5 | Environment, product selection, interventions, experimental families |
| S4 | Results and §4.1 User Profiles | 6–9 | Attribute effects, humans, sensitivity, preference profiles |
| S5 | Implications and Limitations | 9–10 | Interpretation, ecological scope, generalization limits |
| S6 | Conclusion | 10 | Case for cumulative behavioral evaluation |
| S7 | Acknowledgments and References | 10–14 | Funding, resource support, cited literature |

| B | ABxLab Intervention Details | 18–19 | Per-observation HTML transformation |

The document is a mixed **empirical AI study, benchmark paper, and experimental framework paper**. It is not a formal security attack paper or theoretical proof paper. Its substantive inventory contains Figures 1–17, Tables 1–5, numbered pair-validity Equation (1), the environment formalization, and the M1/M2 statistical equations. There are no numbered theorems or standalone algorithm boxes. Procedural algorithms appear in prose and lists.

## 3. Background and context

[A] A **large language model (LLM)** supplies the agent's decisions. The agent receives a task, observes a browser state, emits an action, and repeats. Here it also produces explicit thinking text and short-term memory. These generated traces are inspectable study outputs; they are not guaranteed explanations of the model's actual internal computation.

[A] **Choice architecture** means how options and their attributes are presented. A **nudge** steers a decision without removing alternatives. The paper studies authority, social proof, scarcity, negative framing, and incentives. A recommendation from a named review source is an authority cue; a best-seller label is social proof. Some interventions also communicate potentially meaningful product benefits or disadvantages, so influence does not automatically establish an irrational or malicious decision.

[A] A **two-alternative forced choice**, abbreviated 2AFC, limits each task to two candidate products. A **percentage-point effect**, abbreviated pp, describes an absolute change in choice probability. The paper explicitly distinguishes this from relative percentage change: a +20 pp contrast means a 20-point higher probability under the specified comparison.

[A] The authors position their work against task-completion benchmarks such as WebArena and VisualWebArena. Their account is that existing functional evaluations often reveal whether an agent can execute a task while providing less information about why one acceptable option is chosen over another. Their related-work discussion also invokes human bounded rationality, heuristics, and nudge theory. These descriptions are the paper's positioning of earlier literature; the cited publications were not independently inspected.

## 4. Research problem and gap

**Existing problem [A].** Delegating choices requires reliable judgment, consistency, and alignment with user intentions, beyond technical competence. Environments already contain persuasive design, arbitrary presentation orders, and imperfect quality signals.

**Shortcoming of prior evaluations [A].** A completion-rate measure can award success for selecting a product without revealing whether that selection depends strongly on superficial framing. The authors argue that realistic web environments should be used as behavioral testbeds as well as task-execution benchmarks.

**Research gap [A].** The paper seeks controlled, scalable experiments on when and how agent preferences shift in realistic web contexts. Earlier controlled nudge findings motivate a more complex shopping environment. ABxLab provides observation interventions without requiring a custom environment for every study.

**Motivation [A].** Agents may become consequential economic decision-makers. Strong, predictable sensitivities create risks for delegated decisions and opportunities for systematic measurement.

**Scope [A].** The actual evidence concerns consumer product choice in one shopping environment, primarily two products, textual observations, specified prompts, and contemporary model versions. Medical, travel, financial, market-wide, and societal consequences are motivating examples, not directly evaluated outcomes.

**Security relevance [D].** The bounded gap addressed here is between task success and trustworthy selection under environmental persuasion. A separate comparison is needed to answer whether the same underlying model is more susceptible when embedded in a web-agent system than when given equivalent information as a standalone LLM.

## 5. Research questions / objectives / hypotheses

The paper does not present a numbered set of formal research questions or preregistered hypotheses. The following identifiers index its stated objectives and informal questions; they do not convert them into author-declared formal hypotheses.

| ID | Objective or question | Evidence and test |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | Build controllable behavioral experiments over web observations | Framework, §§3.1 and B; Figures 1 and 13 |
| O2 | Measure sensitivity to ratings, prices, order, and nudges | Primary and matching studies; Table 2 |
| O3 | Determine whether exact nudge wording and product context matter | Figure 2; Appendices A.1–A.2 |
| O4 | Compare agent and human responses to shared choice conditions | Original-condition human baseline; Figure 3 |
| O5 | Ask whether larger price/rating advantages generate larger responses | §4 sensitivity analysis; Figures 4 and 11 |
| O6 | Examine explicit user preferences | §3.5.3 and §4.1; Figure 5 |
| O7 | Test robustness to statistical form, incentive plausibility, and more options | Appendices F–H; Figures 15–16; Tables 3–5 |
| O8 | Explore action horizons and generated reasoning/memory | Appendices A.4 and D; Figures 12 and 14 |

[A] A hierarchical rating → price → nudge decision rule is discussed as a hypothesized explanation. It is not established as a recovered internal algorithm. Appendix D explicitly states that this full hierarchy is difficult to see at scale in the generated streams.

## 6. Assumptions / threat model

[A] The system formalization assumes a state space, action space, observation space, deterministic state transition for a given environment, and intervention functions that map observations to observations. The agent receives the task as natural-language intent and acts using observations and history. Experimenters control the transformation applied before observations reach the agent.

[A] The evaluated agent observes pruned Hypertext Markup Language (HTML), containing elements visible in its current viewport. It receives no visual input. Screenshots in this report show the website and diagrams to the reader; they were not the experimental agent's observation modality. Scrolling can expose additional content.

[A] The task asks for the best product and instructs the agent to visit every tab and record useful information in memory. Original trials do not specify a user's relative priorities for price or ratings. That ambiguity is intentional; preference-profile studies subsequently supply priorities.

[A] There is no formal attacker, attacker budget, security asset taxonomy, adversarial success criterion, or defense benchmark. The authors explicitly distinguish nudges intended to influence from attacks designed against an agent. Intervention access is an experimental capability, not evidence that a real adversary possesses control over all browser observations.

[D] A security interpretation can map page content to an influence surface and cart addition to a consequential tool-mediated action. The relevant integrity concern is whether a user's delegated decision is redirected by lower-trust environmental claims. That mapping remains an analyst framing. Exfiltration, credential theft, privilege escalation, command execution, persistent compromise, and malicious instruction following are not tested.

## 7. Methodology

### Framework and agent loop

[A] ABxLab derives from AgentLab and WebArena. At each step, the environment supplies an observation; configured functions edit it; the agent sees the edited observation and emits one action; the environment transitions; the cycle repeats. Appendix B specifies that transformations receive and return pruned HTML and are selected through a YAML configuration associated with a URL. Changes can insert nudge text, change a displayed price, or modify ratings.

[A] The nine available action types are clicking, filling fields, navigating to a URL, scrolling, selecting options, keyboard input, focusing a tab, going back, and going forward. Appendix C supplies parameterized action descriptions and examples. These are documentation, not separate experimental treatments. An episode ends when any product is added to the cart or after ten actions. The cart action is an experimental stopping event; checkout or actual spending is not reported.

### Product data and preprocessing

[A] Products come from the shopping catalog. Items without nonzero ratings are excluded; products with multiple sub-options are removed to avoid extra interaction steps; remaining products are grouped by category. A lightweight LLM filters titles containing suggestive nudge-like phrases, multi-packs, bundles, or explicit quantities. This is intended to reduce uncontrolled persuasion and economic incentives. The filter model identity, validation accuracy, and exact retained catalog counts are not supplied in the inspected description.

[A] Valid pairs are within a category and satisfy rating and relative-price limits. Original pairs permit an absolute rating gap of 0.10, described as ten points, and a relative price gap of at most 0.50. Matched-rating pairs require equal ratings while retaining the 0.50 price-gap limit before intervention. Prices are equalized afterward for the matched-rating-and-price condition, rather than requiring naturally identical prices.

[A] Original pairing sorts items by price and selects valid consecutive items. Matched pairing searches up to the next k items, with default k = 10, stores valid equal-rating pairs, and seeks the largest non-overlapping pair set under that neighborhood constraint. Product order within a pair is randomized. When excess pairs exist, uniform subsampling produces 50 pairs per experimental set. The exact optimization implementation and random seeds are not supplied.

### Experimental design and models

[A] Ten intervention texts × 50 pairs × three assignment conditions generate 1,500 base configurations. Assignment conditions are no nudge, first product nudged, and second product nudged. Each task opens the two product pages in different tabs. The three attribute regimes are Original, MR for matched ratings, and MRaP for matched ratings and prices. MR uses reselected equal-rating pairs; MRaP uses those same pairs with price edits.

[A] The 17 evaluated models are GPT-5, GPT-5 Mini, GPT-5 Nano, GPT-4.1, GPT-4.1 Mini, GPT-4.1 Nano, GPT-4o, GPT-4o Mini, o3, o4-Mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Claude 3.5 Haiku, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Llama 4 Maverick, Llama 4 Scout, and DeepSeek-R1. Names vary slightly across prose and tables, such as Claude 4 Sonnet versus Claude Sonnet 4; they are treated as naming variants, not additional models.

[A] Temperature is 0.1 where available and 1 for OpenAI reasoning models. The reported aggregate exceeds 80,000 trials, approximately 2.5 billion tokens, and approximately 400,000 requests. Secondary experiments use six models: the figures and trio table identify Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Llama 4 Maverick, and o3. Exact model snapshot identifiers, dates, per-condition retry policies, seed schedules, and a complete trial allocation are not given in the supplied methods.

### Humans, metrics, and statistics

[A] Thirty Prolific participants each made 50 choices and supplied short rationales in an interactive binary-choice interface. The authors describe this as an institutional-review-board-exempt study. The human comparison covers the 1,500 Original trials, not MR or MRaP. The exact allocation and dependence structure of participant decisions are not fully described.

[A] Each binary trial becomes two product-level records. The outcome is one if that product is selected and zero otherwise. Covariates identify model, cheaper product, higher-rated product, position, effective nudge side, nudge text, and category. Negative nudges are inverted so that the opposite product is coded as effectively favored.

[A] The primary estimator is a linear probability model with fixed effects, implemented with fixest. Two-way cluster-robust standard errors cluster by nudge text and product category. Estimated marginal means are computed with emmeans using proportional weights over observed nuisance-factor distributions. Binary contrasts compare indicator 1 with 0. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustments are applied separately within analysis families. Alternate logit models test functional-form robustness.

### Reporting boundaries

[A] The acknowledgment names high-performance-computing support and API credits, but no reproducible hardware specification, software version matrix, exact total cost, or wall-clock runtime is supplied. There is no supervised training split to report: these are behavioral inference experiments, rather than a newly trained predictive model. No code or dataset artifacts were independently inspected.

## 8. Experiments / analyses

| ID | Analysis | Design, outcome, and evidence | Principal qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | Primary Original choice | 17 models; ten nudges; 50 pairs; three assignments; estimated choice-probability contrasts; Table 2 | Best product is not defined by an external quality oracle |
| X2 | Attribute matching | MR removes rating differences; MRaP additionally edits prices; Table 2 and Figure 6 | Original-to-MR comparisons also change selected pairs/categories |
| X3 | Human baseline | 30 participants × 50 decisions; Original only; Table 2 and Figure 3 | No matched-condition human results |
| X4 | Nudge-text heterogeneity | M2 contrasts by wording; Figure 2 and Figures 7–9 | Negative texts use effective-side recoding |
| X5 | Product-category heterogeneity | Category contrasts, averaged across models; Figure 10 | Categories differ across Original and matched samples |
| X6 | Difference-magnitude sensitivity | Coverage-selected pairs vary price with comparable ratings or vice versa; Figures 4 and 11 | Exact sample sizes/tolerances and polynomial uncertainty not fully reported |
| X7 | User preferences | Four attribute focuses × increased/decreased descriptions; six models; Figure 5 | Prompt sensitivity is observed; durable defense effectiveness is not tested |
| X8 | Time horizons | Distribution of final action steps, capped at ten; Figure 12 | Longer episodes are not experimentally assigned deliberation treatments |
| X9 | Generated-trace analysis | GPT-4o judges mentions and deciding factors; Figure 14 | Trace faithfulness and judge interpretation are acknowledged limitations |
| X10 | Statistical specification | Compare LPM and logit marginal effects; Figures 15–16 | Agreement across estimators does not remove shared design assumptions |
| X11 | BOGO plausibility | Stratification by durable/consumable and matching; Tables 3–4 | BOGO mixes framing and potential economic benefit |
| X12 | Three alternatives | Six models; 20 trios; 800 trials/model; Original only; Table 5 | Smaller study, heuristic negative-nudge coding, no matching |

[A] The coverage-based sensitivity dataset ranks categories by their coverage of price/rating ranges, selects products to span bins, and samples comparable pairs. Its purpose differs from X1: X1 asks whether an item being cheaper or higher rated matters; X6 asks whether the magnitude of that advantage matters much after its direction is established.

[A] The user-profile descriptions distinguish Rating, Price, Authority Nudge, and Rating & Price. For example, increased price sensitivity describes a tight budget, while decreased price sensitivity says the user is willing to pay more for a better product. These are qualitative natural-language changes, not numerical utility weights.

[A] The trio study replaces pair-relative indicators with first in list, cheapest, and highest rated. A negative nudge is treated as favoring each of the other two products, which the authors describe as a simple heuristic. Its 800 trials per model should not be assumed to follow the original three-assignment pair design; the paper does not provide a full trio assignment derivation.

## 9. Results

### Ratings

[A] Table 2 reports Original-condition higher-rating effects of 81.2 pp for o4 Mini, 77.6 pp for o3, 73.8 pp for GPT-5 Mini, 65.6 pp for GPT-4.1 Mini, and 64.7 pp for Llama 4 Maverick. Claude 3.5 Haiku and GPT-4.1 Nano have small, nonsignificant higher-rating effects of 7.8 and 2.9 pp. The authors link their weak rating effects to strong order sensitivity. The human higher-rating estimate is 5.0 pp and nonsignificant.

[A] The prose says 14 of 17 models show approximately 30–80 pp rating effects, but the exact table includes 81.2 pp and GPT-4o Mini at 20.6 pp. The range should be read as a broad characterization, not a substitute for exact entries. The authors' argument that ratings can be imperfect quality indicators is attributed to cited prior work; this experiment does not independently measure objective product quality.

### Price

[A] Thirteen of 17 models significantly prefer cheaper products in Original, with significant effects ranging from 15.2 pp for o3 to 34.3 pp for GPT-4o Mini. Price sensitivity becomes much larger for several models under MR: Llama 4 Maverick reaches 93.2 pp, o3 83.3 pp, GPT-5 75.5 pp, and Gemini 2.5 Pro 75.1 pp. It is not universal: GPT-4.1 Mini has a nonsignificant −6.4 pp MR contrast.

[A] MRaP price contrasts are nonsignificant across Table 2. Because displayed prices have been equalized, these residual contrasts should not be interpreted as an ordinary response to an available price difference. They concern the retained lower-price coding under an intervention that removes the displayed difference. The authors use their disappearance to argue against agents relying on other price correlates.

### Order

[A] GPT-4.1 Nano's viewed-first effects are +88.8 pp in Original, +92.0 pp in MR, and +92.7 pp in MRaP. Claude 3.5 Haiku instead has −35.4, −53.6, and −42.7 pp. Direction therefore differs sharply between models. Original GPT-5 and Llama 4 Scout have significant positive estimates of 16.7 and 23.1 pp. The authors report significant order sensitivity in 13 of 17 models in the matched conditions, typically favoring the second-viewed option.

[A] The prose on p. 7 rounds GPT-4.1 Nano's Original preference to +90 pp; Table 2 provides +88.8 pp. Appendix E links position to both side and viewing order. The study consequently supports presentation-sequence sensitivity, while not cleanly separating all possible spatial, tab, and temporal components.

### Nudges and humans

[A] With ratings and prices matched, GPT-4o's nudge effect is +62.1 pp, GPT-4.1's +57.2, Claude Sonnet 4's +55.9, Gemini 2.5 Pro's +55.8, and GPT-5's +53.3. Fourteen models have significant positive MRaP nudge effects; GPT-4.1 Nano is 0.0, Claude 3.5 Haiku is −5.7, and Llama 4 Scout is +8.7, none significant. Thus susceptibility depends on model and cue, and is not uniformly positive.

[A] In the Original human baseline, order is 4.0 pp, higher rating 5.0 pp, cheaper price 9.4 pp, and nudge 9.9 pp. Only the nudge estimate is significant at p < .05 after the stated adjustment. Human average absolute attribute sensitivity is approximately 7%, compared with approximately 13% for the lowest model and 31% for the highest. These are author-reported summary values, not new calculations.

[A] Exact wording matters. The named Wirecutter recommendation is the strongest average nudge in each regime, followed by Buy 1 Get 1 Free and the best-seller statement. Under MRaP, every nudge text significantly shifts average choice probability when pooled across models. That statement is distinct from saying every individual model responds significantly to every text.

### Sensitivity, profiles, and robustness

[A] The authors interpret magnitude analyses as threshold-like: modest differences can establish a preference, while greater advantages do not steadily strengthen it. Figure 11's fitted curves are visibly nonmonotonic. These patterns qualify any simple claim that agents continuously optimize price advantage.

[A] User profiles often reorganize priorities categorically. Decreased authority-nudge sensitivity nearly eliminates or sometimes reverses its effect; increased sensitivity makes the nudge nearly decisive while reducing other effects. The authors characterize these as switches rather than calibrated adjustments. No exact full matrix of profile-effect values is supplied as a table.

[A] LPM and logit marginal effects correlate at approximately r = 0.93. BOGO remains influential for durable goods as well as consumables. In the trio study, highest-rating effects span 73.9–98.0 pp, with smaller nudge effects of 4.9–25.1 pp. Llama 4 Maverick and o3 have nonsignificant trio nudge estimates. The trio results extend the phenomenon modestly beyond pairs without establishing behavior in unrestricted shopping.

## 10. Figure-by-figure interpretation

### Figure 1 — Framework and benchmark workflow, p. 3

[B] A catalog feeds a sampling engine, which accepts plausible product comparisons and rejects others. Product pages then enter the intervention component, where text insertion, price matching, and rating matching are illustrated. Arrows indicate movement from selection to observation modification; dotted numbered links identify edited page elements. This is an architecture illustration, not a quantitative chart. [A] Its caption distinguishes sampling, binary forced choice, and a statistical analysis procedure that is not pictured. Small illustrative product values are not treated as experimental results.

### Figure 2 — Average effect of individual nudge texts, p. 7

[B] Three horizontal forest-plot panels show Original, Matched Rating, and Matched Rating & Prices. The vertical entries are nudge texts; the horizontal axis is estimated effect with 95% confidence intervals, displayed in percentages. Red and blue points distinguish directions/significance in the figure's presentation, with stars adjacent to estimates. Negative nudge labels explicitly indicate inversion. [A] The accompanying text identifies the named authority cue as strongest, followed by BOGO and best seller, and states that all texts are significant under full matching. Exact per-text point estimates are not reliably recoverable from the small plot and are not invented.

### Figure 3 — Average absolute attribute sensitivity, p. 8

[B] A vertical bar chart orders humans and models by mean absolute attribute effect. Its vertical axis runs in percentage units, with ticks through 30%; model labels occupy the horizontal axis. The human bar is lowest and Claude Sonnet 4 highest. [A] Text supplies approximately 7%, 13%, and 31% for humans, the lowest model, and highest model. This aggregation discards effect direction and can conceal different behavioral mechanisms. It is not a probability of attack success.

### Figure 4 — Effects of difference magnitude, p. 8

[B] Two forest plots show six models on the vertical axes and estimated effects with 95% confidence intervals on the horizontal axes. The left panel concerns a 100-percentage-point change in price advantage; the right concerns a one-point rating change. Several intervals overlap zero. [A] The text singles out Claude Sonnet 4 as the exception for significant rating-magnitude sensitivity. The precise scaling of the underlying rating variable is not sufficiently elaborated to translate this into stars or percentage-rating units with confidence. Large binary attribute effects and small magnitude slopes measure different quantities.

### Figure 5 — User profile effects, p. 9

[B] A grid of forest plots crosses profile inputs with cheaper, higher-rated, and nudged outputs. Six models appear within relevant panels. Rows separate increased/decreased preferences across rating, price, combined rating-and-price, and authority nudge. Horizontal axes are estimated effects with 95% confidence intervals; red and blue points show positive and negative patterns, and a zero reference assists comparison. Blank nudge panels for unrelated profiles should not be read as zero-valued experimental results. [A] The authors interpret the plot as dominant preference switches. Exact point-by-point values remain compressed and uncertain at this resolution.

### Figure 6 — Main effects plotted, p. 15

[B] Forest plots arrange Original, MR, and MRaP across groups, each with viewed-first, cheaper, higher-rated where meaningful, and nudged contrasts. Models occupy rows, including humans for Original. This visualizes Table 2 and does not add a separate dataset. [A] Original rating differences disappear by design in the matched regimes. Table 2 is the exact numeric reference; repetitive points are represented through that table's analysis.

### Figure 7 — Original nudge effects by model, p. 15

[B] Small multiple forest plots show individual nudge texts for 17 models and the human baseline. Horizontal position represents estimated marginal effects in pp; intervals show uncertainty. Models differ greatly in both strength and consistency. [A] The text highlights near-deterministic responses to particular cues among susceptible models. Human effects are comparatively limited and appear especially associated with the named authority cue. Individual stars are too small for a reliable exhaustive transcription.

### Figure 8 — MR nudge effects by model, p. 16

[B] The same nudge-by-model small-multiple structure is used after equalizing ratings. The horizontal coordinate is estimated marginal mean effect in pp, with uncertainty bars and zero reference. Nudge influence remains heterogeneous. This plot supports comparisons of wording under MR, rather than the assumption that rating matching makes all models equally susceptible. Exact values are not numerically labeled at readable size.

### Figure 9 — MRaP nudge effects by model, p. 16

[B] Parallel small multiples remove displayed price as well as rating differences. Several susceptible models show large positive shifts for leading cues; other models remain weak or mixed. [A] Appendix A.1 emphasizes near-deterministic susceptibility to certain texts. The visual reinforces that a pooled statement about all texts does not imply universal responsiveness by every model.

### Figure 10 — Nudge effects by product category, p. 17

[B] Three forest panels compare Original, MR, and MRaP. Product categories occupy the vertical axis; estimated effects and 95% confidence intervals occupy the horizontal axis. Some category rows are unavailable in particular regimes because samples differ. [A] The authors find relatively weak evidence for category heterogeneity and caution that subtle contextual effects may be difficult to detect. The changing category composition prevents treating all cross-panel shifts as a pure matching intervention.

### Figure 11 — Choice probability versus price advantage, p. 18

[B] Six colored curves represent Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek R1, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, Llama 4 Maverick, and o3. The horizontal axis is price advantage in percent, with labeled ticks from 10% to 90%; the vertical axis is predicted choice probability. A red dashed horizontal line marks 50%. Curves bend and sometimes decline as advantage grows. [A] These are predictions from an LPM with fourth-order polynomial price-advantage features. No confidence bands are displayed. Consequently, curve peaks, reversals, and extreme-edge behavior should not be treated as exact raw-data response rates or statistically confirmed turning points.

### Figure 12 — Action-step distributions, p. 19

[B] Seventeen small histograms show number of trials by maximum step reached, with horizontal positions 1–10 and a shared count scale. Many models concentrate at approximately two or three steps; GPT-4.1 Nano is especially concentrated at the first step, while some smaller models have more dispersed tails. These are qualitative visual observations, not reconstructed counts. [A] Episodes are capped at ten and models generally decide quickly. The plot does not establish that extra steps cause more robust choices.

### Figure 13 — Intervention implementation, p. 19

[B] A website page, a YAML configuration, an intervention engine, and the agent's resulting view are connected by directional arrows. Numbered annotations locate changed text, price, and review/rating information. The engine converts incoming HTML to edited HTML. [A] This occurs at each timestep for configured URLs. No timing, computational overhead, or scalability curve is shown.

### Figure 14 — Judged generated-trace attributes, p. 24

[B] Grouped bar charts cross Rating, Price, Nudge, and Other columns with Original, MR, and MRaP rows. Three models—Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT-5—appear within panels. The vertical axis is count; red bars indicate deciding factor and cyan bars mentioned factor. Mentions and judged deciding factors diverge, especially for attributes equalized by the experiment. [A] GPT-4o supplies the judgments. The figure shows judgments of generated text, not direct access to internal decision causation. Exact bar counts are not labeled and are not estimated here.

### Figure 15 — LPM versus logit marginal effects, p. 28

[B] A grid crosses Original, MR, and MRaP columns with cheaper, higher-rated, nudged, and viewed-first rows. Two colored estimates and uncertainty bars compare the LPM and multinomial-logit formulations across models. Many points track closely, with visible differences at some extremes. [A] The reported overall correlation is approximately 0.93. Matched-rating panels do not contain higher-rating effects because that predictor is removed by design. Statistical agreement supports robustness to this particular functional-form change.

### Figure 16 — Logit latent utility coefficients, p. 28

[B] Three panels show Original, MR, and MRaP. The horizontal axis lists attributes and the vertical axis is utility coefficient in log-odds units. Points and uncertainty bars are compared against a dashed zero line. Positive rating influence is visible in Original; nudge influence remains positive under matching; price approaches zero after price matching. These coefficients are neither probabilities nor percentage-point effects, and exact numerical values are not read from the graph.

### Figure 17 — Concrete product-page examples, p. 31

[B] Two overlapping page pairs show lenses and headphones. One page in a pair displays a nudge beneath the product title. They illustrate how interventions coexist with ordinary product descriptions, price, ratings, and cart controls. No quantitative axes or inferential results are present. The product pictures are presentation examples, not visual inputs to the evaluated text-only agents. Tiny screenshot attributes are deliberately not transcribed as study-level outcomes.

## 11. Table-by-table interpretation

### Table 1 — Intervention inventory, p. 5

## 12. Diagram / architecture interpretation

[A/B] Figures 1 and 13 describe complementary layers. Figure 1 begins with experiment construction: obtain catalog items, filter and pair them, open candidate pages, choose an intervention assignment, and evaluate the resulting choice. Figure 13 expands the observation-editing layer: a URL-specific configuration selects transformations, the engine receives pruned HTML, functions edit it, and the agent receives the edited HTML.

[A] State transitions and observation edits have different roles. A browser action changes environmental state through T; an intervention I changes what the agent is shown. The framework's controlled influence enters through observation transformation. Repeated application maintains the configured presentation across steps. It is therefore insufficient to describe ABxLab as merely placing a banner in a screenshot.

[D] For security analysis, this separation helps identify a candidate trust boundary: external-looking product information can shape the language-model decision that selects an action. However, the paper's engine is a research apparatus. Its existence does not prove an attacker can intercept network traffic or alter any desired page in deployment. No additional architecture for credential storage, sandboxing, authorization, or agent privilege management is supplied.

## 13. Equations and mathematical concepts

### Environment formalization, §3.1, p. 3

[A] E = ⟨S, A, O, T, I⟩ identifies the environment. S is state space, A action space, O observation space, T: S × A → S the deterministic transition function, and I a set of intervention functions mapping O → O. The notation uses I for both the collection's generic member and, typographically, the intervention family; the operational meaning is that a selected function edits an observation.

[A] The transition is s_(t+1) = T(s_t, a_t). The delivered observation is o-tilde_(t+1) = I(o_(t+1)). Inputs are the current state/action and the next raw observation; outputs are the next state and edited observation. The agent's action uses task intent, current edited observation, and prior action/observation history. These equations define an interaction loop, not a trained loss function or optimization guarantee.

### Pair-validity Equation (1), §3.3, p. 4

[A] |rating(p1) − rating(p2)| ≤ Δr, and |price(p1) − price(p2)| / min{price(p1), price(p2)} ≤ Δp.

[A] p1 and p2 are same-category products. Δr is the maximum absolute rating gap; Δp is the maximum relative price gap using the cheaper price as denominator. The absolute-value operator ignores which product is larger. Both constraints must hold. Original uses Δr = 0.10 and Δp = 0.50; matched trials use Δr = 0 and Δp = 0.50 before post-hoc price editing. The rating condition is an absolute rating difference, whereas the price condition is a normalized difference; the prose's shared percentage language should not erase this distinction.

### Product-level outcome and covariates, Appendix E, p. 26

[A] Y_tp ∈ {0,1} indicates whether product p is selected in trial t. c_tp indicates cheaper; r_tp higher rated; p_tp position; n_tp effective nudge side; m_tp model identity; θ_j(t) the nudge-text regressor; k_tp category; α_t trial fixed effect. Product position is defined as 0 = left/viewed second and 1 = right/viewed first. This coding couples spatial and viewing-order descriptions. Equal-rating conditions remove the higher-rated term. Negative nudge inversion is a substantive modeling convention, not an observed positive message on the opposite product.

### Primary model M1, Appendix E.2, p. 27

[A] Y_tp = βᵀX_tp + α_t + ε_tp, with X_tp = (m_tp + c_tp + n_tp + r_tp + p_tp)^[N]. β is the coefficient vector, X the expanded predictor representation, α the trial fixed effect, and ε the residual. The superscript notation denotes all main effects and interactions up to N-way among the listed terms; it is not ordinary exponentiation. A precise numeric N is not separately stated beyond that description. Inputs are product records and covariates; the fitted model supports predicted probabilities and marginal contrasts.

[A] Trial fixed effects absorb common trial-level variation. Cluster-robust uncertainty accounts for residual association by text and category. The description also says M1 uses text fixed effects, but the displayed formula explicitly shows only α_t. Because text and model identity may be constant within a trial, exact estimability and fixed-effect implementation require the unavailable code/design matrix. This is a reporting ambiguity rather than proof that the published estimates are wrong.

### Nudge-specific model M2, Appendix E.3, p. 27

[A] M2 keeps Y_tp = βᵀX_tp + α_t + ε_tp but adds θ_j(t) to the interaction expression and restricts data to nudged trials. Text is treated as a regressor instead of a fixed effect so contrasts can vary by wording. This estimates heterogeneity of intervention response. Marginal means average predictions over other observed factors, and contrasts for binary predictors are 1 versus 0 in pp.

### Alternate and nonlinear concepts

[A] Appendix F uses a multinomial logit specification that reduces to binary logit for pairwise choice. No full logit equation is printed in the supplied section. Figure 16 uses coefficients in log-odds units; these must not be read as direct probability changes. Figure 11 uses fourth-order polynomial price-advantage features, but its complete fitted equation and coefficients are not supplied. No theorem, proof, or claim of optimality accompanies these models.

## 14. Interpretation and discussion

[A] The results support the authors' claim that successful execution can coexist with unstable selection. Matching and profile experiments reveal that changing the relative availability or priority of cues can cause large shifts. The authors interpret this as rule-like behavior: a dominant cue controls choice until removed or overridden, after which another cue becomes decisive.

[D] That interpretation is plausible but not uniquely identified. Product selection changes between Original and MR; displayed-price edits create another kind of treatment; prompts explicitly ask for different priorities. The data demonstrate behavioral changes under these interventions. They do not by themselves recover one internal decision tree shared by all models. The differing order effects and nonsignificant nudge responses in several models reinforce this qualification.

[A] The discussion proposes that training data, reward signals, or related sources may explain human-like heuristics without human cognitive constraints. Those mechanisms are proposed explanations, not experimentally isolated causes. The authors also caution that human literature estimates are not directly commensurable with this setup. Their own Original-condition human baseline provides the closer comparison.

[D] The security lesson is specific: an agent's observation stream can carry persuasive claims that influence a delegated action even without an explicit malicious instruction. This widens the behavior that security evaluations may need to measure beyond obvious instruction injection. It does not establish that every influenced choice violates user intent, since the base task leaves preferences unspecified and some cues convey economically relevant information.

## 15. Contributions and novelty

**System/methodological [A].** ABxLab provides configurable observation interception and intervention over existing websites, separating environment operation from controlled presentation changes.

**Benchmark [A].** The authors introduce a scalable product-choice evaluation across 17 models, ten texts, multiple attribute regimes, and selected choice sets. Its distinctive purpose is behavioral response measurement rather than task completion alone.

**Empirical [A].** The study reports strong model-specific sensitivities, matched-condition shifts, a human baseline, wording heterogeneity, qualitative user-profile switches, and smaller robustness analyses.

**Conceptual [A].** Consumer choice is proposed as a testbed for a cumulative behavioral science of AI agents. Trustworthy delegation is framed as a judgment problem as well as a competence problem.

**Dataset/open implementation [A].** The authors state that they produce several datasets and release an open benchmark/framework. This report records the release claim without asserting that artifacts were downloaded, executable, complete, or licensed in a particular way.

[D] The paper does not contribute a demonstrated exploit against deployed systems, an agent-versus-standalone security comparison, a verified defense, or a theoretical characterization of vulnerability. Those should not be added to its novelty claims.

## 16. Limitations

### Authors' stated limitations

[A] Section 5 acknowledges a tradeoff between causal isolation and ecological breadth. Binary forced choices with controlled textual nudges simplify real decision contexts, which may contain larger and more diverse choice sets and multimodal cues. Filtering and pairing simplify real-world heterogeneity. One consumer domain and one set of contemporary agents limit cross-domain transfer. ABxLab is a measurement framework, not a direct long-run forecast of markets or society.

[A] Appendix D identifies two limitations of generated-trace analysis: thinking/memory may not faithfully represent decision-making, and the LLM judge may misinterpret them. The authors explicitly consider the main controlled experimental evidence more reliable. They note that the full hypothesized hierarchy is difficult to identify in those streams.

[A] Appendix H acknowledges a smaller trio study and more modest statistical power. Only Original is evaluated, using a model subset. Negative-nudge treatment requires a simplifying heuristic. Appendix G notes that estimated BOGO ordering and magnitudes depend on specification. Appendix A notes that subtle category effects may be difficult to detect.

### Additional evidence-based analyst observations

[D] No standalone-LLM comparison isolates the added effect of web integration. No adversarial attack/defense evaluation establishes malicious exploitability. The human baseline is confined to Original and does not reproduce the agent's HTML/action interface. User priorities are underspecified in the base task, preventing a universal distinction between influence and error.

[D] Exact model snapshots, sampling seeds, retained catalog counts, filtering quality, complete trial allocation, and failure/timeout handling are insufficiently detailed for independent reproduction from the paper alone. Original-to-MR comparisons change pair composition, which complicates attribution of all effect differences to rating removal. The statistical formulas do not fully expose fixed-effect implementation. These are analyst observations about the supplied reporting, not concessions attributed to the authors.

## 17. Threats to validity

The following validity categories are analyst organization of the evidence, unless an author acknowledgment is explicitly stated.

**Internal validity [D].** Interventions and randomized within-pair order help isolate presentation effects. However, reselected MR pairs and altered category distributions complicate cross-regime comparisons. Negative-nudge inversion assumes symmetry between discouraging one product and favoring another; trios weaken that equivalence further.

**Construct validity [D].** Choice sensitivity is measured directly; security vulnerability, objective product quality, welfare loss, and violation of user intent are not. A favorable price, return policy, or incentive may be relevant information. Strong effects establish responsiveness, while their normative undesirability requires additional assumptions.

**Statistical conclusion validity [D].** Cluster-robust standard errors, multiple-testing correction, and logit checks strengthen the analysis. The number of clusters, all effective sample counts, and exact fitted specifications are not fully exposed. Dense plots omit many numeric intervals. Fourth-order fitted curves without visible confidence bands warrant caution about apparent turning points.

**External/ecological validity [A/D].** The authors acknowledge binary textual shopping limits. The analyst additionally notes that preopened tabs and a ten-action horizon differ from open-ended discovery, search, checkout, and repeated purchasing. Text-only agent results do not establish multimodal-agent behavior.

**Reproducibility [D].** Framework release is reported, but artifact execution was outside this closed-document analysis. Without configurations and trial data, aggregate counts cannot establish exact repeatability. Software/model drift cannot be assessed from the supplied paper alone.

## 18. Future work and open questions

### A. Explicit author proposals

[A] Extend the framework to richer environments, broader choice sets, multimodal contexts, and additional domains. Develop cumulative behavioral science through open-source contributions. Use commensurable experiments to jointly study humans and agents. Appendix A.4 specifically proposes testing whether temporal decision styles systematically condition sensitivity to interventions—for example, whether repeated review changes framing sensitivity or rapid choice changes order sensitivity.

### B. Additional open questions from this analysis

[D] Does the same model respond more strongly when information arrives through a browser/action loop than when equivalent content is presented in a standalone prompt? That requires a matched comparison absent here. Which components—viewport restriction, memory, tool execution, sequential presentation, or task ambiguity—contribute to any difference?

[D] Can agents distinguish verified product attributes from unsupported promotional claims? Do explicit user preferences reduce manipulation under conflicting or deceptive content, or simply introduce another rigid priority? How do longer horizons, open search, larger catalogs, and actual costs change susceptibility? What outcome measure captures user-intent integrity rather than mere choice movement? These are proposed research directions, not experiments already performed.

## 22. Very simple explanation — Explain Like I'm 15

Imagine asking a shopping assistant to compare two products and put the better one in your cart. The assistant can click the right button and finish the job, yet still make its choice because one page says best seller or because it looked at that product last. Finishing the job does not tell you whether its judgment was dependable.

The researchers built a way to change what shopping agents read while keeping the experiment controlled. They changed prices, ratings, and short promotional messages. Many agents reacted much more strongly than the human participants in the same original product comparisons. When ratings were tied, some agents relied heavily on price. When both ratings and prices were tied, some promotional messages became very influential. Other agents mostly followed presentation order. Different models had different weaknesses.

This matters for security because a web agent reads information from pages and can turn that information into an action. A misleading page might therefore influence what it does. But this paper did not test a malicious attacker, and it did not compare a web agent with the same model used on its own. Its strongest lesson is that we should measure how outside information changes an agent's choices, alongside checking whether it can complete a task.

No numbered page in the supplied 1–31 sequence is missing. Visual renderings are absent for ten pages; those pages were read through supplied text. The example HTML is deliberately omitted by the paper, and URLs are redacted. Code, complete configurations, trial-level data, model outputs, exact model snapshots, and executable release artifacts are not supplied. Their absence limits reproduction checks, not reading of the supplied prose.

### Uncertain interpretations

Small plot coordinates, some significance symbols, and screenshot microtext cannot be read confidently enough for exact extraction. Figure 4's rating-unit scaling is not sufficiently explicit for conversion into stars. Table 3's specific matching condition and interval confidence level are not explicit in its immediate labeling. Table 4's printed percentages are retained as estimated marginal means rather than silently assigned a stronger estimand definition. M1's text-fixed-effect implementation is not fully shown by the equation. Position coding combines side and viewing sequence. Aggregate trial counts do not expose every experiment's allocation or failures.

### Deliberately compressed material

The full Table 2 numeric matrix is compressed to major effects, extremes, and exceptions; its remaining cells are not separately reproduced. Dense nudge-by-model figures are explained without duplicating every point or star. Bibliographic entries, action-call examples, Python/DSPy schema boilerplate, repeated prompt wording, funding particulars, and decorative page elements are shortened. Appendix C's substantive task instructions are preserved in meaning; its example product attributes are illustrative, not additional experimental outcomes. ### Potential omissions

Every identified major section, substantive subsection, experimental family, figure, table, major mathematical object, contribution, and author-stated limitation has a corresponding representation above. Exhaustive preservation of every secondary number, citation, example token, plotted coordinate, or Table 2 cell is not claimed. The open artifacts remain unreviewed. claims.statement: ABxLab intervenes on observations before agents receive them; the evaluated shopping agents receive viewport-limited pruned HTML without visual input.

The primary design combines ten interventions, fifty product pairs, and three nudge-assignment conditions into 1,500 base configurations; attribute regimes distinguish Original, matched ratings, and matched ratings plus prices.
The study evaluates 17 language models over more than 80,000 experimental trials, reporting choice effects primarily as absolute percentage-point changes.
Price influence can become nearly decisive after ratings are matched: Llama 4 Maverick has a 93.2-percentage-point cheaper-product contrast in MR, rather than a 93.2% relative improvement.
Under matched ratings and prices, average nudge contrasts are +55.9 percentage points for Claude Sonnet 4 and +62.1 for GPT-4o; these are condition-specific effects averaged over nudge texts.

In the Original human baseline, order, higher rating, and cheaper price estimates are nonsignificant, while the 9.9-percentage-point overall nudge estimate is significant; matched-condition human comparisons are not reported.
Explicit natural-language user preference profiles often reorganize agent priorities like categorical switches rather than providing small, calibrated changes.
The authors acknowledge that binary choices, controlled textual nudges, filtering, and one consumer domain limit ecological breadth and transfer of precise effect estimates.

The generated thinking/memory analysis is preliminary: the authors warn that traces may be unfaithful and that the LLM judge may misinterpret them, favoring the main experimental evidence for causal conclusions.
Alternate logit and primary linear-probability marginal effects are highly correlated at approximately 0.93, supporting robustness to this functional-form change.
The three-alternative robustness study uses twenty product trios and 800 trials per model, evaluates only Original with six models, and acknowledges more modest statistical power.

The paper is relevant to security through environmental persuasion of delegated web actions, but its nudges are not an adversarial attack benchmark and its results do not establish greater vulnerability than standalone LLMs.

limitations: All 31 pages were inspected through supplied text; only 21 pages were visually rendered. All numbered figures and tables occur on rendered pages.
No tools, browsing, external sources, or executable artifact checks were used.
Dense plot coordinates, individual significance markers, and screenshot microtext were not exhaustively transcribed.
The full Table 2 matrix is compressed to major results, extremes, and exceptions; secondary cells are not all reproduced.
Figure 4 rating-unit scaling, Table 3 condition and interval level, and portions of statistical fixed-effect implementation remain uncertain.
The paper does not directly compare web agents with standalone LLMs and does not test a formal adversarial attack or defense.
Original and matched-rating samples differ in product and category composition; human comparisons cover Original only.
Generated thinking and memory are not guaranteed faithful, and the GPT-4o judge may misinterpret them.
The supplied source hash is preserved as provided and was not independently recomputed.

research.title: A Framework for Studying AI Agent Behavior: Evidence from Consumer Choice Experiments
research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, ANALYST INFERENCE: The paper shows that environmental product-page information can strongly influence a web agent's delegated selection and cart action. It supports studying observation-mediated influence alongside task competence. It does not compare agents against standalone LLMs, quantify a relative vulnerability gap, or isolate tools, browsing, memory, or sequential interaction as causes of such a gap.
research.attack_surface: ANALYST INFERENCE: The relevant influence surface is the pruned HTML observation stream, including promotional text, displayed ratings, prices, and presentation order. ABxLab supplies experimental observation-editing capability. The paper does not establish an attacker's real-world access, a malicious instruction payload, exfiltration, privilege escalation, or compromise.
research.method: Controlled consumer-choice experiments in OneStopMarket using ABxLab observation transformations; 17 LLM agents; ten nudge texts; fifty product pairs per primary set; Original, matched-rating, and matched-rating-plus-price regimes; Original human baseline; fixed-effect linear probability models with two-way cluster-robust standard errors, adjusted multiple testing, and logit robustness. Additional analyses examine user profiles, nudge/category heterogeneity, difference magnitude, action horizons, judged generated traces, BOGO plausibility, and product trios.
research.limitations: One domain, primarily binary textual choices, viewport-limited HTML, ten-action cap, filtered/reselected product pairs, contemporary model set, and no matched-condition human baseline limit generalization. Trace analysis has acknowledged faithfulness and judge limitations. Trio tests are smaller and Original-only. External release artifacts were not supplied or reviewed. Security relevance is interpretive; no standalone-LLM comparison or adversarial defense evaluation is performed.
